title: The Dead and the Dying
teaser: Gogol anatomizes Russia's 'dead souls.' Tennyson mourns the passing of Arthur. Browning's Duke speaks of his murdered Duchess. Cole paints allegories of life's voyage. Comte declares the death of theology. From Moscow to Manchester, souls are counted — and found wanting.

art.label: Art
art.content: In Rome, Thomas Cole completes the second version of The Voyage of Life — four allegorical paintings tracing human existence from infancy to old age along the 'River of Life.' A voyager guided by an angel passes from sheltered childhood through ambitious youth, turbulent manhood, and finally acceptance of death. Cole founded the Hudson River School, America's first indigenous art movement, which saw the untamed American wilderness as the nation's equivalent of Europe's ruins — nature as sacred text. But The Voyage of Life is explicitly Christian allegory: the youth reaches for a shimmering castle in the sky (ambition's illusion), the man prays amid tempests (faith as survival), the old man glimpses angelic light through parting clouds (death as transcendence). Cole painted this in Rome — an American artist, in the heart of Catholic Europe, creating Protestant allegory using the language of Renaissance masters.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Nikolai Gogol publishes Dead Souls — a satirical 'poem in prose' following the conman Chichikov as he travels provincial Russia buying rights to dead serfs still listed on tax rolls. The title operates on two levels: literal (deceased peasants as legal property) and spiritual (the moral vacancy of the landowners who trade them). Gogol intended a Dantean trilogy — Inferno, then Purgatorio, then Paradiso — but burned the manuscript of Part Two shortly before his death, leaving only provincial Hell. In England, Tennyson's Poems establishes him as the nation's foremost poet; his 'Morte d'Arthur' presents the dying king passing Excalibur to Bedivere as the old order dissolves. Robert Browning's Dramatic Lyrics includes 'My Last Duchess' — the Duke of Ferrara coolly describing a portrait of his murdered wife. All three works centre on death; all three mask violence behind formal beauty.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Auguste Comte completes the sixth and final volume of his Cours de philosophie positive, fully articulating positivism: the doctrine that human thought progresses through three stages — theological, metaphysical, and finally positive (scientific). In the positive stage, questions of ultimate causes are abandoned; knowledge comes only from observable phenomena and their laws. Comte coins the term 'sociology' and proposes that scientific method, having mastered nature, should now reorganise society. The Cours is philosophy as funeral oration: the death of theology, the death of metaphysics, the birth of what Comte calls 'social physics.' Meanwhile, in March, Stendhal dies in Paris — the author of The Red and the Black, that cold dissection of ambition, passing almost unnoticed. His literary executor called him 'the most improbable of geniuses.'

hist.label: History
hist.content: On 29 August, the Treaty of Nanking ends the First Opium War. Britain forces China to cede Hong Kong, open five treaty ports, and pay twenty-one million silver dollars. The 'unequal treaties' begin — the mechanism by which European powers will carve concessions from the Qing Empire for a century. In Britain, the Chartist general strike erupts from August to September — up to half a million workers across the industrial Midlands stop work, pulling plugs from steam boilers to halt the factories. It is the largest industrial action of the nineteenth century, demanding universal male suffrage and workers' rights. The strike is crushed, its leaders transported. On 30 March, Dr Crawford Long in Georgia performs the first surgery using inhaled anaesthesia (diethyl ether) — but fails to publish, leaving the 'discovery' to others. Pain, like souls, proves negotiable.
hist.funFact: Queen Victoria became the first reigning British monarch to travel by train on 13 June 1842, riding the Great Western Railway from Slough to Paddington. She reportedly found the experience 'delightful.'

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year's theme is the enumeration of souls — and what counting reveals. Gogol's plot depends on Russia's census system: serfs ('souls') were taxed until the next revision, meaning dead peasants remained profitable on paper. The Chartists demanded that every man be counted equally through universal suffrage. Britain's income tax (newly established this year) counted wealth. The Treaty of Nanking counted silver, ports, and territory seized. Cole's allegory counts the stages of a single soul's journey. Comte's positivism counts only what can be measured, declaring all else illusion. Charles Dickens, touring America this year, met Edgar Allan Poe in Philadelphia — two masters of death and the uncanny, briefly crossing paths. The connections are not coincidence but symptom: industrial capitalism was creating a world measured by abstractions — labour-hours, tax rolls, commodity prices — while artists and philosophers struggled to find where the human soul might still reside.
